12.0.0.en: The Lord sent Nathan the prophet to David after a period since his sin of not less than a year, for Bathsheba his wife had borne him a child, who lived for a time, as will come in (vv. 14, 15). This shows that God teaches the prophets to be humble: although David was a prophet, He did not speak to him directly but sent another prophet to him to rebuke him, to declare to him the voice of God, and to call him to repentance. Nathan related to him a case for David to judge between two men, one very rich and the other poor, living beside him. Most likely Nathan took David aside while he was giving his opinion on this case, in order to reveal his sin to him through it so that he would repent. This is the fitting way of reproving others: that it be in private, lest we embarrass them before people.

12.1.0.en: Nathan went on to recount the case, saying that the rich man had very many flocks, but the poor man had nothing except one ewe lamb, and he cared for it until it grew up in the midst of his household. It was dear to him, sharing his food, and he loved it like his daughter.

12.2.0.en: He spared to take of his own flock to dress for the wayfaring man: he was unwilling to slaughter one of his own sheep to cook a meal for the guest.

12.2.1.en: Nathan completed the rest of the case, saying that it happened that the rich man received a guest, and he was unwilling to take one of the many sheep he owned to slaughter it and prepare a meal for the guest, but with all cruelty seized the one ewe lamb that the poor man owned and slaughtered it to honor his guest with it.

12.3.0.en: David was greatly moved when he heard the case on which Nathan asked for his judgment, and he was very angry at what the rich man had done and issued a severe sentence against him. He swore by the living God that the man should be put to death for the monstrousness of his crime and should restore the lamb fourfold according to the Law (Ex 22:1), because this man had no pity on the poor man. Thus David's anger against this man appears: he went beyond the limits of the Law, which was to fine him by restoring four times what was stolen, to killing him because he was a hard-hearted man. And this was indeed fulfilled in David: just as Uriah the Hittite died, four of David's sons died, namely the son of Bathsheba (the child of sin), Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. And just as David committed adultery with Bathsheba, Amnon committed adultery with Tamar his sister, and Absalom with his father's concubines. God forgave David and did not put him to death because he offered repentance from the depth of his heart and was not ashamed to confess before Nathan the prophet.

12.4.0.en: Nathan, like the other prophets of God, did not fear to confront King David with the word of the Lord which He had charged him to deliver to him, despite its harshness. He rebuked him, declaring to him that he was the rich, hard-hearted man mentioned in this case, and reminded him that God had taken him from his father's house to be king over Israel, and had rescued him many times from Saul's pursuit of him, and had given him as an inheritance the servants of Saul and all his house and his wives, that is Michal the daughter of Saul, and everything that was his passed to him. He was not content with making him king over the tribe of Judah only, but made him king over all the tribes of Israel; and if this was not enough for him, and he wanted more, He would have given him that too. This speech shows Nathan's courage in rebuking David, because by it he exposed himself to David's anger, so that he might order him killed; but he was laying down his life when he obeyed God and rebuked David.

12.5.0.en: After that Nathan confronted David openly with his sin, which was his despising of God's commandments and his killing of Uriah with the sword of the children of Ammon, that is, plotting with Joab to kill Uriah by placing him in the face of the battle to die, and afterward taking Bathsheba, with whom he had committed adultery and who had conceived.

12.5.1.en: And here David understood that the case Nathan had presented to him was his own story: he was the rich man with the many cattle, which signify his many wives, and he had seized the one ewe lamb of the poor man, that is Bathsheba, the only wife of Uriah the Hittite.

12.5.2.en: At last David awoke from the hardness of heart and the spiritual blindness that had covered him after his fall into adultery and murder. Despite David's righteousness, his negligence made him fall into the gravest of sins; and it is the nature of sin, when it increases, to deprive a person of his spiritual sense, so he remained a whole year without repentance until Nathan the prophet roused him. The Holy Bible mentions this shameful sin of David for the following reasons:

12.5.3.en: 1- It does not flatter the saints but shows their weaknesses, so that we may be encouraged however much we fall.

12.5.4.en: 2- Let us thank God, who keeps us when we see others, especially the strong, fall.

12.5.5.en: 3- Let us be encouraged, if we fall into sin, to repent like David.

12.5.6.en: 4- We learn the depth of repentance, whatever our sins may be, so that we press on with power in the way of God.

12.5.7.en: 5- A declaration of humanity's need for the Christ the Savior, for all are exposed to falling, even the saints.

12.5.8.en: 6- Acceptance of divine discipline if He allows it, so that our repentance may be complete, as happened with David through the death of his infant son and Absalom's driving him out of the kingdom, in addition to many other troubles.

12.5.9.en: God uses parables with you to rouse you to repent of your sins, so do not neglect them as though they were ordinary stories. Benefit from the events that pass over you, such as the death of one of your loved ones, or a problem that happens to you or to someone you know, so that it may be a means of your repentance; then God will accept you and remove your sins from you, however heavy they may be.

12.6.0.en: The sword shall never depart from thine house: the stability of peace in his house will be shaken, so there will be quarrels and troubles among the members of his family, and his descendants will kill one another.

12.6.1.en: And now the Lord has decreed to punish you with the following:

12.6.2.en: First: as you handed Uriah over to be killed, the sword will work to shake the peace in your house (God does not cause evils but permits them to occur). This punishment was fulfilled afterward: Absalom killed his brother Amnon (ch. 13) and then launched a coup against his father (ch. 15). It was fulfilled also in Solomon's killing of his brother Adonijah, and likewise many harsh wars arose afterward against the kingdom of Judah, and finally its people were taken captive to Babylon; and before the captivity, the sons of the last of the kings of Judah, of the descendants of David, namely King Zedekiah, were killed by Nebuchadnezzar, who killed his sons before his eyes.

12.7.0.en: The second punishment that God permitted for David was the rising of evil against him from his own house, through Absalom's taking the kingdom from him and driving him out of it (ch. 16:8). The third punishment was the assault on his wives, and this was fulfilled by his son Amnon's assault on his sister Tamar (ch. 13) and then Absalom's lying with his father's concubines and the announcing of this before the people, that is, it would be “in the sight of this sun” (ch. 16:21), meaning that he declared before all his seizing of the kingdom from his father.

12.8.0.en: David committed his sin with Bathsheba and worked to have her husband killed, all of this in secret, but the Lord declares to him that He will carry out his punishment openly.

12.8.1.en: The following appears in God's punishment of David:

12.8.2.en: 1- God's justice and His showing no partiality to anyone, whatever his worldly position or his nearness to God.

12.8.3.en: 2- The evil influence of the head of a family upon it: after David sinned, his children were affected, so Amnon committed adultery with his sister and Absalom killed his brother.

12.9.0.en: After Nathan confronted David with his sin, he felt it and repented of it, and acknowledged his guilt before the Lord Himself and in the presence of the man of God Nathan, and he wrote the fifty-first Psalm, which begins with the words “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness.” ...... And since Nathan judged that his confession had come from sincere repentance, he told him, by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, that God had forgiven him: although his sin deserved the punishment of death according to the Law, God spared him from death because of his repentance of it. It is clear that this is a picture in the Old Testament of the sacrament of confession: just as a person confesses before his father of confession and his sin and its punishment, which is death, are lifted from him, so God lifted from David his sin and its punishment because of his confession before Nathan the prophet, who is a type of the father of confession.

12.10.0.en: The whispers of the guards must have passed on the matter of David's sin and made it a subject of gossip, so the rumors spread and perhaps reached his enemies. Here they saw David, the man godly in the Lord's eyes, collapse before sin, and they showed their malicious joy over him. Therefore, although God removed David's sin from him and spared him from death, He punished him, as Nathan declared to him, with three punishments, and the fourth is that the child who would be born of Bathsheba would die, because he was the fruit of sin.

12.10.1.en: If the door of repentance is open to you however grievous your sins, like the sin of David, why do you delay? Rise, hasten to your father of confession so that you may escape eternal destruction, regain your peace, and enjoy fellowship with God.

12.11.s.en: (3) The child of adultery and the birth of Solomon

12.11.0.en: Nathan departed from the king's presence and returned to his house. Then the child that the wife of Uriah the Hittite bore to David fell sick, and the sickness grew severe upon him.

12.12.0.en: David fasted, prayed, and humbled himself before the Lord that the child might be healed, and instead of lying on his royal bed, he slept on the ground as a form of austerity and humbling before God. What increased David's humbling was his feeling that the child's sickness was discipline from God for his adultery and murder.

12.13.0.en: The chiefs of his people and the men close to him tried to raise him from the ground to sleep on his bed and to seat him with them at the table to eat of the delicious royal food, but he did not wish to lessen his humbling before the Lord; most likely he ate only meager foods for austerity and humbling before God. Thus we see the practice of fasting clearly in the depths of the Old Testament, which the children of God now practice in His Church.

12.14.0.en: The child died on the seventh day of his illness, and the members of the king's household were at a loss how to tell him the sad news, for how great was his grief when the child was sick, and how much more it would increase if he learned of his death. He would surely be shocked on hearing the news and would deprive himself of food and rest more than before.

12.14.1.en: And we note that God permitted the death of the child to declare that there is no gain from sin, but every gain that comes from it must pass away.

12.15.0.en: David sensed, from the movements and whispers of his men, that an important event had taken place, so he concluded that the child was dead, and he asked them whether the child was dead, and they were obliged to tell him the truth.

12.16.0.en: Contrary to what the members of his household expected, David behaved with complete calm on hearing the news. He ended the signs of his humbling, rose, washed, and anointed himself with perfume to regain his refreshment, and put on his royal garments instead of the austere ones he had worn during the mourning. He went to the house of the Lord, where he prayed and worshiped, thanking the Lord in every circumstance, even for the death of his son, and then he returned to his house and ate the usual royal food.

12.16.1.en: David's conduct shows his complete submission to the divine will, and this is what every true believer ought to do, thanking the Lord in every circumstance and in all things, offering the Lord praise and worship.

12.17.0.en: David's men were astonished at his conduct and were bewildered as to what the matter could be, so they dared to ask him how it was that he grieved and humbled himself while the child was still alive, and when he died he rose and resumed his normal life and abandoned all signs of grief!

12.18.0.en: David made them understand that he had humbled himself before the Lord that his son might be healed while he was still alive, being certain that the Lord was able to grant him healing however severe the illness. Although Nathan had told him that the child would die, he did not lose his hope in God's mercy and continued to pray.

12.19.0.en: David added that his son had died and there was no longer any opportunity to ask for God's mercy in his healing, so his thought turned to the eternal life to which his child had gone before him, and he would follow him when God willed. Thus a group of virtues appears in this great man David the prophet, which are:

12.19.1.en: 1- His faith in God's mercy, so he hastened to Him with many prayers that his son might be healed.

12.19.2.en: 2- His inclination to austerity and humbling before God in many spiritual practices, such as fasting accompanied by prayers, with all that it includes of abstaining from food, bodily comfort and splendid clothing.

12.19.3.en: 3- David's reliance on God and acceptance of His will, however contrary to his desires.

12.19.4.en: 4- David's attachment to eternal life, which influenced his life and made him feel a stranger in the world although he was a great king, so that he said, “I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me”

12.19.5.en: (Ps 119: gimel 19), which made him cling to prayer and to meditation on the Law of God.

12.19.6.en: Be sure that your prayers, your fasts and your humbling before God are very precious in His sight, for this means your faith and your love for God more than all that is in the world. He accepts this spiritual striving of yours, and even if He does not give you what you asked, He will give you manifold more in your life, keep you, and give you a great place in the heavens.

12.20.0.en: Solomon: a name meaning peaceful or peacemaker.

12.20.1.en: David comforted Bathsheba on the death of their son, and then he went in to her and she bore him a son whom he named Solomon, as a prophecy of the peace that would prevail in the time of his reign, and the Lord would give him rest from all his enemies. The Lord loved Solomon because of His foreknowledge of the glorious works he would do in the future when he took the throne of the kingdom, and the Lord sent a message to David by the hand of Nathan declaring another name for Solomon, Jedidiah, that is “beloved of Jehovah,” declaring His love for him.

12.21.s.en: (4) The capture of Rabbah of Ammon

12.21.0.en: The royal city: the high part of the city of Rabbah in which the king dwells.

12.21.1.en: The city of waters: the lower part of Rabbah, the capital of the kingdom, which was watered by the Jabbok River, one of the tributaries of the Jordan, and so had abundant water.

12.21.2.en: Joab was fighting the Ammonites, and during that time David fell into his sin. The Holy Bible mentions it in detail because it does not hide the sins of the saints, and then it returns here in this verse to complete the events of the war with the Ammonites.

12.21.3.en: And we note that the Holy Bible is not bound by historical sequence, because it is a spiritual book concerned to show the spiritual meanings so that we may apply them in our lives. So it mentions in this chapter that Bathsheba bore a son, who grew and died, and then she conceived and bore Solomon. Then it returns and tells us about the war with the Ammonites, although the war had ended before the events mentioned in this chapter, that is, the death of the child of adultery and then the birth of Solomon. Joab attacked the capital of the children of Ammon, called Rabbah, which was in two parts; he took the lower part, called the city of waters, and cut off the water from the upper part, called the royal city, in which the king dwelt. Then he besieged the royal city and it began to fall before him, so he sent to David to give him the good news of the fall of the capital of the children of Ammon and asked him to hasten with an army to enter this capital himself, so that the honor of capturing it would be his and not Joab's. Thus God rouses David and restores him to his proper position as a king and military leader working for God's sake, not giving in to the sin and evil into which he had fallen. For repentance and life with God raise a person from sin and restore him, with head held high, to a new life with God.

12.21.4.en: And we note that Joab spoke sharply to David in calling him to fight and take the city, saying, “Come thou... lest I take the city, and it be called after my name.” But he also shows his loyalty to David in wanting David's name to be called upon the city; and so we ought to imitate Joab, ascribing all power and success to God and not to ourselves.

12.22.0.en: David carried out Joab's request, so he gathered the rest of his army and set out toward “Rabbah,” entered it and captured it.

12.23.0.en: A talent of gold: equal to about 8 kg.

12.23.1.en: David took the crown of their king, which was of gold, heavy in weight and set with precious stones, and put it on his head as a declaration of the extending of his authority over the Ammonites. He and his men also took very great spoil from the defeated city “Rabbah.” Most likely, because of the weight of the crown, two of David's men lifted it and placed it on his head for a short time as a declaration of his greatness and his possession of the children of Ammon, and then they lifted the crown from his head.

12.24.0.en: Harrows: an agricultural implement, a cart with toothed wheels for cutting the stalks of wheat and barley.

12.24.1.en: The brickkiln: the furnaces in which mud bricks, that is raw ones, are burned.

12.24.2.en: In view of the Ammonites' harassment of and attack upon the children of Israel more than once, at the hand of Nahash their king (1 Sam 11) and the mockery by his son Hanun of David's messengers (ch. 10), in addition to the hardness of heart of the Ammonites, who clung to pagan gods to the point of offering their children as sacrifices and burning them to please them, David was compelled, contrary to his custom, to be harsh with them. He killed them by passing harrows and saws over their bodies after he had thrown them on the ground, and killed them with axes, and killed some of them in brick furnaces, to be burned and tormented by the blazing fire, perhaps so that this would make the rest of the pagan peoples fear God, abandon the worship of idols, and fear to fight against the people of God.

12.24.3.en: Although God had commanded not to be hostile to the Ammonites, because they are the descendants of Lot, relatives of the people of God (Deut 2:

12.24.4.en: 16-23), yet because of the Ammonites' immersion in pagan worship and their repeated assault on the people of God, David was compelled to attack them and kill them.

12.24.5.en: God is very merciful to everyone who repents and returns to Him, but He is just in punishing the wicked who reject Him, destroying them with eternal destruction. So take advantage of the opportunity of this life to hasten in repentance to God, and you will escape eternal torment.

12.24.6.en: Amnon rapes his sister and Absalom kills him (1) The rape of Tamar and her expulsion (vv. 1-18:) 1 And it came to pass after this, that Absalom the son of David had a fair sister, whose name was Tamar; and Amnon the son of David loved her. 2 And Amnon was so vexed, that he fell sick for his sister Tamar; for she was a virgin; and Amnon thought it hard for him to do any thing to her. 3 But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man. 4 And he said unto him, Why art thou, being the king's son, lean from day to day? wilt thou not tell me? And Amnon said unto him, I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister. 5 And Jonadab said unto him, Lay thee down on thy bed, and make thyself sick: and when thy father cometh to see thee, say unto him, I pray thee, let my sister Tamar come, and give me meat, and dress the meat in my sight, that I may see it, and eat it at her hand. 6 So Amnon lay down, and made himself sick: and when the king was come to see him, Amnon said unto the king, I pray thee, let Tamar my sister come, and make me a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat at her hand. 7 Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, Go now to thy brother Amnon's house, and dress him meat. 8 So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house; and he was laid down. And she took flour, and kneaded it, and made cakes in his sight, and did bake the cakes. 9 And she took a pan, and poured them out before him; but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, Have out all men from me. And they went out every man from him. 10 And Amnon said unto Tamar, Bring the meat into the chamber, that I may eat of thine hand. And Tamar took the cakes which she had made, and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother. 11 And when she had brought them unto him to eat, he took hold of her, and said unto her, Come lie with me, my sister. 12 And she answered him, Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel: do not thou this folly. 13 And I, whither shall I cause my shame to go? and as for thee, thou shalt be as one of the fools in Israel. Now therefore, I pray thee, speak unto the king; for he will not withhold me from thee. 14 Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her. 15 Then Amnon hated her exceedingly; so that the hatred wherewith he hated her was greater than the love wherewith he had loved her. And Amnon said unto her, Arise, be gone. 16 And she said unto him, There is no cause: this evil in sending me away is greater than the other that thou didst unto me. But he would not hearken unto her. 17 Then he called his servant that ministered unto him, and said, Put now this woman out from me, and bolt the door after her. 18 And she had a garment of divers colours upon her: for with such robes were the king's daughters that were virgins apparelled. Then his servant brought her out, and bolted the door after her.
